method.the_one_test_that_reordered_everything: A corner's character at kart road width is set by its DIRECTION CHANGE, not its radius. The widest arc the corridor allows is R_line = R + e*(1+k)/(k-1) with e = (W-1.400)/2 and k = sec(theta/2), clamped so the line's tangent length R_line*tan(theta/2) fits inside the corner's own tangent plus the shorter adjacent straight. The multiplier is 25.3 at 45 deg, 5.83 at 90 deg, 1.00 at 180 deg. Three of the four proposals instead quoted R + W/2 - 0.7 m - the hug-the-inside-edge line, which nobody drives and which is independent of angle. I recomputed every corner in all four layouts on the correct construction. It does not change any regulation gate; it changes which corners are corners, which is the entire racing question. The rhythm proposal is the only one that used it, and its independent verifier reproduced 12 of its 13 lock ceilings to within 0.1 km/h.
sources_used: the four .json layouts and their .md companions
the four independent .verify.json files (all four verdicts: 'major issues')
my own line-radius and apex-speed recomputation over every corner segment in terrain.json and racecraft.json, which the terrain verifier did not do

scores.strongest: It is the only layout whose TWO claimed overtaking spots both survive an independent racing-line recomputation. T9 Il Tornante is 180 deg at a 14 m entry - the widest passing entry anyone produced - so its line is hard-bounded at 20.3 m (the verifier's own minimum-curvature solve returns 20.3 m, i.e. the corner cannot open at all), fed by 220.2 m of tow that the T8 34 deg kink splits into 102.7 + 51.9 m so neither leg breaks the 200 m cap, needing 39.4 m of braking with 51.9 m available (12.5 m of margin, so late braking is genuinely on), exiting onto 126.2 m of +2.8% climb. That is all three of the brief's overtaking ingredients - tow, width, punishing exit - measured, at one corner, immune to the line model that broke most other claims in this exercise.
scores.weakest: The corner vocabulary the whole proposal is named for does not survive. On the verifier's minimum-curvature solve T2 opens from a claimed 34.3 m to 94.3 m, T4 Le Esse from 54.3 to 118.5 m, T10 from 42.8 to 128.1 m and T8 from 114.3 to 283.9 m. Four of ten corners are flat kinks and two more (T6 50.6 m, T7 54.5 m) are 105-113 km/h sweepers rather than the 57.7 and 71.7 km/h corners advertised. The 'eleven rungs of racing-line radius, no two close enough to confuse' collapses to about five real events, and with it the fine-grained lap-time gradient that is supposed to be the reason to drive it for 25 laps.
reasoning: OVERTAKING 26/30. T1 Curva del Banco: 178 m of tow, 12 m of entry width (the regulation maximum for a first corner, correctly used at the maximum), 112 deg of direction change so two lines genuinely diverge, and a DECREASING radius 66 -> 32 m so the defender who covers the inside is committed to the tight half. The braking zone survives the line correction and gets longer: the verifier's geometric line for T1b is 42.1 m (~96 km/h apex) against a 135.9 km/h approach, which is ~35 m of braking rather than the claimed 26.1. T9 as above. Docked 4 because both spots are in the same third of the lap by time and there is nothing in the infield (T5/T6/T7) where a move can be made - the infield is a 57-95 km/h single-file corridor.

STICKS 9/10. 126.2 m of +2.8% climb out of the hairpin and then T10 - a compromised hairpin exit is paid for over 10% of the lap. At T1 the switchback is structural, not asserted: the attacker's outside line through a 112 deg left is the inside line into T2, a right 36.7 m later.

REVERSE 17/20. The strongest reverse case anyone made, and it is measured rather than narrated. Forward there are 2 braking zones over 20 m; reversed there are 6 (24.9 / 35.8 / 32.7 / 20.0 / 17.5 / 18.8 m). T7 La Staccatina reversed is a 32.7 m braking event off a 133.6 km/h descent, at a corner that forward needs 14.0 m and is taken on a lift - a passing place that provably does not exist in the other direction. T3 Il Curvone flips from a 150 deg left to a 150 deg right, 4.17 s at the same 1.83 g, against 2.81 g of rollover margin instead of 2.43 - a 15.6% change on the lap's defining corner for the cost of one authored layout. And the author measured the sector marks rather than assuming they break, found they work (16.26/16.80/16.23 s), and said so. Docked 3 because all eleven kerb spans and both run-off sizings are wrong reversed, and the T10 surface transition moves from 8 m before turn-in to 8 m after the exit, deleting the reverse lap's only surface-step test.

RHYTHM 11/15. Ten direction changes in 1,300 m is 130 m per corner, the busiest of the four, and no straight exceeds 178 m so there is no transport section anywhere. But four of those ten are flat, so what a driver actually meets is T1, T3, a slow infield, T9 and four kinks - less variety than the document sells and, over 25 laps, a lap whose middle third is a single 57-95 km/h corridor.

LEARNABILITY 6/10. T3 Il Curvone (4.17 s at one radius, 130.9 m of constant arc) and T9 (hard-bounded, 3.19 s) are honest and both are corners a driver improves at slowly. The advertised fine gradient - 'T2 is 1.7 m and 2.7 km/h from the cliff' - is the part that failed: at a 94.3 m line radius T2 is not a #137 corner at all, so the promised subtle time is largely not there.

FEEL 8/10. Reads most like a real kart circuit of the four: a 180 deg hairpin, a 150 deg Curvone, a second-gear infield, ten corners, longest straight 178 m. Docked 2 for the terrace - the start/finish plateau sits 8.09 m above the T7 approach with 10.56 m of clear ground between asphalt edges, a 76.7% face over roughly 60 m of each. That is a barrier on both sides of the start straight and both sides of a braking zone, with no verge and no run-off, on a lap-one 8-kart grid.

AI 3/5. The R14 180 deg hairpin is the tightest in the set and is where pure pursuit will corner-cut worst without a speed-scaled lookahead; T1's decreasing radius is the classic tightening-corner understeer case. Le Esse (28 deg pair, 16 m apart) is a mild lookahead-cancellation case but the angles are shallow enough that it barely matters.

scores.strongest: It is the only proposal that designed to the angle rather than the radius - 'seven corners above 80 deg and exactly one deliberate kink' - and it is therefore the only one whose corner inventory survives contact with a real racing line. Its verifier reproduced 12 of its 13 quoted lock ceilings to within 0.1 km/h from drive_probe.gd's own rows. Consequently T3 Il Pozzo is the best single overtaking corner produced by anybody: 45.0 m of braking from the lap's 141.3 km/h peak to a 52 km/h first-gear apex, which is the brief's own 44-49 m ceiling and the only proposal that reaches it; a 12 m entry at 140 deg of direction change, so the racing line (27.3 m, 67.5 km/h lock ceiling) and the defensive half-width line (21.9 m, 53.5 km/h) cannot converge and the defender's ceiling is 1.5 km/h above the corner's own apex speed; and an exit onto 186.7 m of up to +5% climb through five upshifts, which is a drag race the defender starts slower.
scores.weakest: It has one overtaking spot, not two, and the second one requires the pass to already be happening. T1 Ronda's braking zone is 12.0 m - the author states this plainly. The mechanism offered instead is the friction ellipse over 99.5 m of arc (defender 65.3 m line at 1.73 g with 0.367 of longitudinal capability, attacker 81.4 m at 1.39 g with 0.665, so 1.8x the drive for three seconds), which is a real effect and correctly computed, but it resolves a move rather than creating one: you cannot get alongside in 12 m of braking, so you have to arrive alongside off a 164.6 m straight with no slipstream model in the sim. Against the brief's 'AT LEAST TWO GENUINE OVERTAKING SPOTS' that is one and a half.
reasoning: OVERTAKING 20/30. T3 scores full marks on all three ingredients and is the strongest corner in the exercise. T1 is a resolution point, not a creation point. There is nothing else: T2 is an admitted regulation artefact (45 deg, 186 m line radius, 0.78 g), the T4/T5 esse is 9-10 m wide and explicitly a place where both karts have to compromise, T6 tightens onto a 22 m line and punishes anyone who is not on the ideal entry, T7 is driven 27 km/h below its own ceiling on purpose, T8 opens under power. Seven of the eight corners are places to lose time, and one is a place to pass.

STICKS 9/10. 186.7 m of climb through five upshifts on a powerband 5,000 rpm wide is the most convincing 'pass sticks' argument in the set, because it punishes the defender in gear position as well as speed. The author also correctly separates the two: the T3 move is settled 355 m later at T2, which is long enough that a lunge does not simply undo it.

REVERSE 15/20. Genuinely different, and for the right structural reason: the two compounds invert sense. T8 forward is a 45 -> 60 m OPENING exit-discipline corner at the end of the lap; reversed it is the FIRST corner, 77.2 m from the line, CLOSING 60 -> 45 m through 130 deg, entered 26 km/h faster. Forward's #137 detector (T6) disappears reversed and becomes a throttle-timing problem. And the hairpin genuinely improves reversed - approached down the 186.7 m climb at ~138 km/h and braked UPHILL, where the grade adds 0.19 m/s2 and the zone shortens to 41.5 m: longer approach, shorter and more stable zone. Docked 5 because the two load-bearing reverse claims are wrong. The claim that 'every one of the six vertical curves swaps profile when the direction reverses' is geometrically false - vertical curvature is invariant under s -> L-s, a crest is a crest driven either way - so 'all six pass, checked' is not established; VC2 at 900 m sits inside the reverse uphill braking zone at ~138 km/h needing 952 m. And the reverse layout's headline corner, T8 at a 132 km/h turn-in, needs 2.362 g on the widest single arc through the compound (58.06 m); its true ceiling is ~117 km/h, so the reverse lap's hardest corner is 15+ km/h optimistic.

RHYTHM 14/15. This is the lens and it is delivered. Three sectors at 15.049 / 16.048 / 15.398 s with 2 / 11 / 5 gear changes - a sector delta on the HUD means a specific thing in each third. The busy 514 m (d=496 to d=1010) contains 13 gear changes and 6 direction changes; everything either side is one input at a time. There is no transport: the longest straight is 186.7 m and it is the climb out of the hairpin, which is the drag race that settles the pass. Docked 1 for T2, which the author correctly calls a bureaucrat - a corner that exists because a straight cannot be 355 m long.

LEARNABILITY 9/10. The most explicit gradient anyone built. Obvious time first: T1 is a lift not a brake, and the hairpin is 45 m of braking with five downshifts. Subtle time later: the T4/T5 esse costs 0.64 s against the same two radii in isolation because crossing 9.5 m of road in 32.47 m at 104 km/h demands 3.07 g against the kart's 1.86, so both corners get driven from mid-track and there is no way to have both. Very subtle last: T7 is driven at 85 km/h against a 112 km/h ceiling to be on the right of the road for T8, costing 0.196 s to recover 0.17 s - and the author says outright it only pays with someone behind. That honesty is worth more than a manufactured sequence.

FEEL 8/10. Eight corners, a first-gear hairpin, one second-gear corner, longest straight 186.7 m and it is a climb. Reads like a kart circuit. Docked 2 for density: 418.5 x 344.3 m for 1,367 m of track with a 30.92 m minimum separation against a 14 m requirement - the author says it plainly, the layout is not working its site hard, and a kart circuit that spacious starts to read as a road course in plan even when it drives tight.

AI 3/5. The T4/T5 esse is the worst pure-pursuit case in the exercise: two 85-90 deg corners of opposite hand 32.47 m apart, where a lookahead spanning both produces near-zero steering demand and a short lookahead oscillates. T6's decreasing-radius compound is the second. Credit back for being the only proposal that hands an AI speed profile the number it actually needs - the 0.64 s linked-pair penalty - rather than two isolated corner speeds.

scores.strongest: The structural insight is the best one in the exercise and it is the only one that solves the reverse problem at the level of geometry rather than authoring: a corner with a long straight on BOTH sides is a passing corner whichever way you drive it, so build two of them and the reverse layout inherits its passing places instead of having to find new ones. T1 has the 198 m start straight before it and the 195 m back straight after; T2 has the back straight before and 276.7 m of uninterrupted full throttle after (the verifier's independent profile makes it 380 m with no braking event at all). Both are 12 m wide, widened OUTWARD over the last 50 m so the inside edge does not move. Then the two compounds are made opposite in sense - T1 opens and T2 closes forward, T1 closes and T2 opens reversed - so each direction gets one clean drive-away corner and one dive-bomb and they trade places. That is a structural reverse differentiation that costs nothing, and nobody else has one.
scores.weakest: Every number underneath the racecraft argument is wrong in the direction that flatters it, and the central claim inverts. The defensive penalties are computed on the inside-EDGE radius rather than the largest arc that fits in the inner half: T1 claimed 27 m / 66.7 km/h against a measured 51.50 m / 110.3 km/h, T6 claimed 26.5 m / 65.4 km/h against 73.53 m / 131.8 km/h, T7 claimed 24 m / 59.0 km/h against 36.49 m / ~92 km/h. The claimed 38.7, 53.7 and 35.2 km/h penalties are 2x to 30x overstated, and at T1 the author's own free-line figure (48.85 m) is SMALLER than the correctly computed pinned line (51.50 m) - in the document's own frame the defender is faster than the attacker, which is the exact opposite of the thesis. On top of that T6 is flat out (121.56 m line radius, 169.5 km/h at 1.86 g, i.e. above the kart's top speed) and T7's 'deliberate slowness' that concertinas the field onto the start straight is 13-15 km/h absent (49.98 m line, 107-109 km/h, not 94.2). The mechanism the whole layout is named for does not exist as described.
reasoning: OVERTAKING 23/30. The BONES are the best in the exercise even though the argument is not. Two 12 m corners of 98 and 100 deg, each with the maximum legal straight on both sides, plus a 175 deg R16 hairpin with 42.5 m of braking from 136.6 km/h - that is three structurally sound places to pass and it is more than anyone else has. What changes under correction is the mechanism, not the existence: on the verifier's numeric solve T1's free line is 69.2 m (~128 km/h) and the pinned inner-half line is 51.5 m (~110 km/h), so the corners become fast 12 m wide side-by-side sweepers with almost no braking rather than the 105-vs-67 km/h braking duels described. An 18 km/h differential over 98 deg of arc at 12 m of width is still a real pass. Docked 7 because the claimed 18.8 and 20.8 m braking zones largely evaporate (135.8 -> ~128 km/h is single-digit metres), so the layout loses the 'arrive alongside under braking' route entirely and depends on a tow the sim does not model.

STICKS 9/10. 276.7 m of full throttle out of T2 - by the verifier, 380 m with no braking event - is the longest punishment for a compromised exit anywhere in the exercise, and it is 59% longer than what a T1 pass buys, which is a deliberate and correct asymmetry between the two corners. T4's exit onto 111.75 m of +4.38% climb out of a locked axle is the second.

REVERSE 14/20. T4 The Cellar reversed is the best single overtaking corner in either direction in any proposal that does not exist in its own forward lap: 111.75 m of -4.38% descent to 143.7 km/h (the only place in either direction the kart reaches its top speed), a 48.5 m braking zone (the longest anywhere in this exercise), into the same 10 m 175 deg hairpin, exiting onto 319 m of climbing full throttle. Longest tow-in and longest drive-out on one corner. And the compound sense-inversion is genuinely structural. Docked 6 for the honest structural weakness the author frames as a feature: T1 and T2 are the passing corners in BOTH directions. Reverse is the same racing at the same two places with the roles swapped, and 'it inherits it' is efficiency for the designer and repetition for the player. The author also identifies, correctly, that T1 and T2 are the same hand one straight apart, so a T1 pass may be worth nothing because the yielding kart exits already on the correct side for T2 - which by their own admission is an argument, not a measurement.

RHYTHM 8/15. The worst lap of the four to drive 25 times. Seven corners in 1,302 m (186 m per corner) and under correction only four of them are events: T1, T2, T4 and T7. T5 is a 309 m line radius (nothing), T6 is flat, T3 is a fast sweeper. The verifier's independent profile finds a 380 m run from T4's exit to T7's braking point with no braking event in it - that is a quarter of the lap and roughly ten seconds of transport, the single largest empty stretch anybody produced. Two 198/195 m straights on top of that.

LEARNABILITY 7/10. T3 The Rim is a good hard corner - 1.86 g for 2.52 s downhill through 9 m of road with a blind exit, the smallest rollover margin on the property - and 'do not defend' is a genuinely counter-intuitive first lesson that is right for this kart even after the numbers are corrected. But the middle of the lap teaches nothing, and the two lessons that would be most valuable (the T1/T2 defensive penalty) are quantified wrongly, so a player learning from the document learns the wrong sizes.

FEEL 5/10. This is the explicit failure mode the brief names. 198 m and 195 m straights back to back, seven corners, 186 m per corner, four real events per 43 s lap, a 380 m no-braking run, and a bounding box of 377.5 x 331.7 m. It reads as a scaled-down road course. Legal on every gate and wrong in character.

AI 3/5. The R16 175 deg hairpin is the most severe corner-cut risk in the set for pure pursuit. The two compounds have zero straight between their halves, so a fixed-lookahead controller sees one blended arc and misses the sense change. Against that, the layout is otherwise smooth and its long constant-radius sections are the easiest thing in the exercise for a quasi-static profile.

scores.strongest: The site logic is the best reasoning anywhere in this exercise. A quarry is flat benches joined by constant-gradient haul ramps, which is exactly the form R = V^2/K rewards, because a constant gradient costs nothing at any speed and only the four breaks cost R*delta metres of road. Everything else follows honestly from that: the fast half of the lap is dead flat because at 125-138 km/h nothing else fits, the switchback is at the top of the ramp because that is the only place on the circuit where an 8.51% break fits in 18 m, and the bench cross-falls into the hill so it does not undercut its own face. The T4 width argument is the single best-argued number in the exercise: 14 m rather than 8 because at 8 m the same centerline radius gives a 29.3 m line (~1.42 g, wrong side of quarter lock) and at 14 m it gives 32.3 m (~1.59 g, drive_probe's 81.3 km/h row almost exactly). That is width chosen from the vehicle sweep rather than from taste, and it is the method the winning layout should adopt.
scores.weakest: Both claimed overtaking spots evaporate under the correct racing-line construction, and the author states the construction himself - in section 11, item 4, applied to somebody else's file. Recomputed on this layout's own segments: T4 Il Frantoio is 85 deg at 26 m through 14 m of road, which is a 67.7 m line and ~126 km/h, not 80 - the 33 m braking zone becomes about 5 m. T7 Il Ciglione is 90 deg at 18 m through 11 m, which is a 46.0 m line and ~101 km/h, not 56 - the 33 m uphill zone becomes about 15 m. And T2 Il Ciglio, the 'biggest speed change on the lap, 137 to 67 in 37 m', is 45 deg: its line radius is 123 m clamped (143 m unclamped, the author's own figure), so it is flat and the 37 m braking zone is zero. There is not one verified braking zone over 20 m anywhere on this circuit in either direction. Five of seven corners also exceed the measured 1.86 g ceiling on their centerline radius at the claimed apex speed.
reasoning: OVERTAKING 8/30. T4 keeps 8 points because 14 m of entry at 85 deg with 254.9 m of tow is still a place two karts can run side by side even at 126 km/h, and because the T4-right into T5-left switchback 64 m later is a correct and durable 'pass sticks' mechanism that does not depend on the speeds being right. Everything else scores zero: T2 is a kink, T7 is a 101 km/h corner rather than a 56 km/h hairpin, and the circuit has no braking event that a following kart can use.

STICKS 6/10. The two mechanisms are sound in kind. T4/T5: the defender who takes the inside at a right exits on the left of a 64 m apron, which is the wrong side for a 79 m left that is on the throttle throughout. T7: the exit is the top of the hill onto 188 m of falling start straight with no corner in between to hide in, and the crest inside the corner takes 11.8% of load off the driven axle exactly at the throttle application. Both survive the line correction; both are attached to passes that will not have happened.

REVERSE 5/20. The reverse layout is not legal. The two Il Salto vertical curves overlap by about 13 m driven backwards, and the reverse T2 braking zone still overlaps a vertical curve - which is the exact defect the author claims, at length and with a redesign, to have fixed. Section 9's 'all six vertical curves pass forwards and in reverse' is the document's proudest claim and it is not true. Beyond legality, the reverse passing spots (T6 reversed off a 132 m -7.81% descent, T2 reversed at the top of an 8% climb) inherit the same evaporation as their forward selves. Credit 5 for the genuinely valuable finding underneath it - that R = V^2/K is speed-dependent and speed is direction-dependent, so the vertical-radius validation has to run once per authored layout rather than once per ribbon, and two earlier versions of this layout were legal forwards and illegal reversed in ways invisible from the forward direction.

RHYTHM 9/15. 'Two flat halves joined by two hills' is a legible structure and the 8% descent versus 7.81% climb pairing is a real contrast - accelerating into a compression versus braking uphill into a blind crest. But with five of seven corners flat under the correct model, the 44 s lap is close to a flat-out loop with one real corner in it, and 192 m per corner is the loosest spacing of the four. Longest straight 196.92 m, which contains 132.28 m of vertical curve.

LEARNABILITY 6/10. 'Brake later than you think at the top of the ramp' is the best single learnable anyone wrote and it survives correction: 132 m of +7.81% climb into a corner invisible until you are in it, where braking is 1.61 g effective against the 1.53 g flat-ground reference the driver's right foot has learned, so everyone brakes early for their first ten laps. Nothing else on the lap has a second layer, because nothing else on the lap is a corner.

FEEL 7/10. The quarry reads as a real place and the terracing gives it more identity than any of the other three. Against that, seven corners in 1,341 m with a 33.76 m minimum separation and a 399 x 360 m box is loose, and the corrected speed profile - almost everything above 120 km/h - is not what a kart circuit feels like.

AI 4/5. Structurally the friendliest of the four for a quasi-static profile: flat benches and constant-gradient ramps mean the grade term is piecewise constant, and the corners are shallow and well separated. The only awkward geometry is T7's two 45 deg halves with the 8.51% grade break at their junction, where the speed profile has to unload 0.118 g at the apex of the tightest corner on the lap.

best_corners.corner: T3 Il Pozzo (16.5 m, 140 deg, 12 m wide) and its 45 m braking zone
best_corners.why: The only braking zone anybody produced that reaches the brief's own 44-49 m ceiling: 141.3 km/h (the lap's peak) to a 52 km/h first-gear apex in 45.0 m on a -1.92% descent, with five downshifts in it. 140 deg of direction change means the line is hard-bounded - racing line 27.3 m against a defensive half-width line of 21.9 m, and the defensive line's 53.5 km/h lock ceiling is 1.5 km/h above the corner's own apex speed, so defending IS scrubbing. Exit onto 186.7 m of up to +5% climb through five upshifts.
best_corners.how_to_graft: Pietrarossa's T9 is already a 180 deg / 14 m hairpin with the right ingredients but only 51.9 m of approach after the T8 kink, so its 39.4 m zone has 12.5 m of margin. Take rhythm's APPROACH, not its corner: replace the 51.9 m post-kink run with a longer descending shelf so the zone is created by arrival speed rather than squeezed into what is left over, and adopt rhythm's first-gear apex so the gearbox is a fifth variable at the one corner where the clutch is already a control (#38).

best_corners.corner: T4 Rampa / T5 Sella, the linked esse (30 m / -90 deg then 34 m / +85 deg, 32.470 m apart)
best_corners.why: The only corner pair in the exercise whose compromise is a measured number rather than a feeling: crossing the full 9.5 m of usable road in 32.47 m at 104 km/h demands 3.07 g against the kart's 1.86, so at 1.0 g you get 3.10 m of the 9.5 and both corners are driven from mid-track. The pair costs 0.64 s against the same two radii in isolation (T4 falls from a 114.1 km/h ceiling to 100.0, T5 from 117.8 to 100.3). That is the whole content of a linked sequence, quantified.
best_corners.how_to_graft: Pietrarossa's Le Esse is the same idea at 28 deg per half, where the line opens to 118.5 m and the pair becomes a flick at 130+ km/h - the matched-hand rollover-asymmetry test (2.43 g left vs 2.81 g right at the same 1.82 g) survives, but nothing else does. Re-cut Le Esse to 85-90 deg per half at rhythm's spacing and keep the matched radii and identical kerbs. The asymmetry experiment then happens at a radius the kart cannot open away from, and the sequence acquires a real linked-pair penalty.

best_corners.corner: The compound sense-inversion: T1 The Anvil opens forward and closes reversed; T2 The Kettle closes forward and opens reversed
best_corners.why: The only reverse-layout differentiation in this exercise that is structural rather than narrative, and it costs nothing to author. Each direction gets exactly one pass-and-drive-away corner and exactly one dive-bomb, and they trade places. Every other reverse case in the set is 'the corners change hand', which is a real physics change on this kart but is the same change everywhere.
best_corners.how_to_graft: Pietrarossa's T1 already inverts from decreasing to increasing radius, and the author noticed. Do it deliberately at a SECOND corner - T10 La Cesta is the candidate, since at 52 deg it opens to a 128.1 m line and currently does nothing in either direction. Recut it as a compound whose sense inverts, so the reverse lap gets its own dive-bomb rather than borrowing T9's.

best_corners.corner: T4 The Cellar driven in reverse - 111.75 m of -4.38% descent to 143.7 km/h into a 175 deg R16 hairpin, 48.5 m of braking, exiting onto 319 m of climbing full throttle
best_corners.why: Longest tow-in and longest drive-out on the same corner, the only place in either direction the kart reaches its top speed, and a corner that does not exist in the forward lap. It is the strongest single argument in the whole exercise for shipping a reverse layout as content rather than as an option.
best_corners.how_to_graft: Pietrarossa's Salita del Tornante already becomes a 126.2 m -2.8% descent into the hairpin reversed, with 35.8 m of braking. Steepen it toward racecraft's 4.4% and lengthen it so the reverse approach reaches the top speed the forward lap never sees, and the reverse hairpin becomes the headline corner of the second layout instead of a slightly better version of the first one's.

best_corners.corner: T7 Il Ciglione's uphill blind braking zone - 132 m of +7.81% climb into a 90 deg corner with 62 m of sight at 1,190 m, 44 m at 1,210 m and 31 m at turn-in
best_corners.why: The single best learnable anyone wrote, and it is the one terrain claim that survives the racing-line correction (46 m line radius, ~101 km/h, still a real corner). Braking uphill is 1.61 g effective against the 1.53 g flat-ground reference a driver's right foot has learned, so the braking point is later than it looks and the corner is invisible until you are in it. Both errors point the same way: everyone brakes early for ten laps, and the fix is worth real time.
best_corners.how_to_graft: Pietrarossa's Salita del Tornante is 126.2 m of +2.8% into T10 La Cesta, and T10 currently opens to a 128.1 m line so nothing happens there. Steepen the climb and put the corner over the crest rather than after it. The resurfacing joint that T10 exists for is a grip step under braking; a crest is a load step at the same instant, and the two together give the corner a reason to be a corner instead of a kink.

best_corners.corner: T4 Il Frantoio's WIDTH DERIVATION (14 m rather than 8 m)
best_corners.why: Not the corner - the method, which is the best-argued number in the exercise. Width was chosen from the vehicle sweep: at the 8 m regulation floor the same centerline radius gives a 29.3 m racing line at about 1.42 g, which is the wrong side of quarter lock and #137; at 14 m it gives 32.3 m at 1.59 g, which is drive_probe.gd's 32.64 m / 1.59 g / 81.3 km/h row almost exactly. Width is the free plausibility lever the regulation hands you, and this is the only place anyone used it as a physics control rather than as a gesture at 'open as much as possible'.
best_corners.how_to_graft: Apply it to Pietrarossa's two passing corners. T1 is 12 m because the regulation caps a first corner at 12; T9 is 14 m by assertion. Re-derive both from the sweep - state the line radius each width buys, the g it lands on, and which drive_probe row it sits between - so the widths defend themselves the way terrain's does.

best_corners.corner: T8 Il Ciglio (110 m, 34 deg) used as a straight-splitter
best_corners.why: The right answer to the 200 m cap and worth stealing whoever wins. 102.74 + 65.28 + 51.86 m of physical run with a 34 deg direction change in the middle: the full 220.2 m tow into the hairpin, and neither leg over 200 m. Every proposal fought the 200 m rule; this is the only one that beat it without losing the tow. It also gives #139 a curb strike above 120 km/h once a lap, twenty-five times in a Final.
best_corners.how_to_graft: Already in the winner. If rhythm or racecraft is preferred instead, this is the first thing to import: racecraft's 198 and 195 m straights are legal and dull, and a 34 deg kink at a 110 m radius in the middle of a longer run buys the same tow with something to get wrong.

best_corners.corner: T9 Il Tornante (14 m centerline radius, 180 deg, 14 m wide) - keep it exactly as it is
best_corners.why: The only corner in the exercise where all three of the brief's overtaking ingredients are present, measured, and immune to the racing-line correction that broke most other claims. 220.2 m of tow, 14 m of entry (widest in the set), 180 deg so the minimum-curvature solve returns 20.3 m and the line cannot open at all, 39.4 m of braking needed against 51.9 m available so late braking is genuinely on and a lock-up lands in the mandatory axial gravel, exiting onto 126.2 m of +2.8% climb. Reversed it becomes a 35.8 m downhill braking duel instead of a braking-and-traction one.
best_corners.how_to_graft: No change. This is the corner the rest of the lap should be built to feed.

concerns: THE BRIEF'S BIGGEST DEFECT: Part 4's walk defines geometry on the CENTERLINE, but Part 2's entire corner vocabulary ('r ~ 55 m the sweet spot', 'r ~ 30-35 m right ON #137's boundary') is a statement about the radius the kart actually drives. The brief never says which one to quote. Three of the four proposals resolved it as R + W/2 - 0.7 m, the hug-the-inside-edge line, which has no dependence on direction change and which nobody drives. That one ambiguity produced the largest error in every proposal - terrain's T2 is 26.8 m by that rule and 143 m by geometry, a factor of 5.3 - and it is the reason all four verify.json verdicts are 'major issues'. Specify the construction: R_line = R + e*(1+k)/(k-1), e = (W-1.400)/2, k = sec(theta/2), clamped so R_line*tan(theta/2) fits inside the corner tangent plus the shorter adjacent straight.

Part 2's corner vocabulary is indexed by radius alone, and radius alone does not determine a corner. At 9-12 m of road, anything under about 80 deg of direction change is flat whatever its radius: the (1+k)/(k-1) multiplier is 25.3 at 45 deg against 1.00 at 180 deg. The table as written actively pushed designers toward shallow corners that read as slow on paper and are flat in the kart. It needs an angle column, or a line that says 'a corner is a direction change, not a radius'.

The brief requires at least two genuine overtaking spots and describes them as being made of '(a) a long enough straight for a tow' - but there is no slipstream in the sim. src/core/vehicle.h has one drag term per kart with no awareness of any other kart. At 138 km/h drag is about 617 N and a 25% tow is worth up to 4.5 m/s of closing over 195 m, which is the whole difference between arriving alongside and arriving behind. Every tow-length number in all four proposals is currently worth exactly zero, and the brief asks for a layout property the vehicle model cannot express. It should say so, and the winning layout should ship with a ticket for it.

The rollover figures (2.43 g left / 2.81 g right) are presented as a reason the reverse layout is a physics change, and three proposals leaned on them heavily. The measured sustained lateral ceiling is 1.86 g - a 31% margin on the worse side. No corner in any of the four proposals gets within 25% of tipping. The asymmetry is real and worth an A/B, but it is not a racing constraint at 1.86 g and the brief let it be treated as one.

The steering-lock sweep's three 0.25-lock rows differ in THROTTLE as well as in lock (0.30 / 0.60 / 1.00). Radius, speed and throttle are confounded, so every 'quarter-lock ceiling' in all four documents is an interpolation across a confounded experiment. Rhythm flags this; the brief presents the table as clean and calls it 'the single most important table here'. The sweep needs a constant-throttle re-run before any of these layouts is committed to track.json.

The braking-distance table is flat-ground only. All four proposals put braking zones on 2.8% to 8% grades and each derived the grade correction independently and slightly differently (1.61 g uphill, 1.45 g downhill, 0.19 m/s2 additive, ...). Give the grade-corrected form once, or four layouts will disagree about the length of the same braking zone.

The self-intersection gate - 14 m between centerlines for points more than 40 m apart along the lap - is a plan-view test only, and it passes layouts that cannot be built. Pietrarossa clears it at 20.56 m while those same two sections are 8.09 m apart VERTICALLY across a 76.7% face with 10.56 m of clear ground: no verge, no run-off, a retaining wall and barriers on both sides of roughly 60 m of start/finish straight and 60 m of a braking zone, on a lap-one 8-kart grid. The gate needs a vertical companion, and this is the binding constraint on any layout with real elevation. It is written down nowhere in ARCHITECTURE.md, REFERENCES.md or the brief.

ARCHITECTURE section 11 says elevation is there 'for looks AND because it loads the tires', and the brief repeats it. Racecraft and terrain independently derived that R = V^2/K is algebraically a cap on vertical acceleration at K/12.96 m/s2 - 0.157 g concave and 0.118 g convex, at ANY speed, because the v^2 cancels - and the same article then says to increase R further in braking and curved sections. A legal Grade 1 kart circuit cannot swing normal load by more than -11.8% / +15.7% anywhere. Elevation on a kart circuit is a visibility feature. The second half of section 11's justification is wrong and should be corrected before it shapes a fifth layout.

Part 3 requires three sectors of roughly equal TIME and separately makes reverse a first-class layout, but never says whether the reverse lap gets its own sector marks. Three of the four proposals discovered independently that it must, and one (instrument) measured that the forward marks happen to survive reversal while still being wrong for a different reason - they put both halves of a paired test in one sector. Say it in the brief so it lands in track.json's schema rather than in four separate prose sections.

Two arithmetic slips worth fixing at source: the brief gives the 81.3 km/h concave radius as 331 m where REFERENCES.md correctly has 330 m, and REFERENCES.md gives the 21.2 km/h concave radius as 23 m where 21.2^2/20 = 22.47 -> 22 m. The second is the row you read to size a compression at the #137 cliff speed.
summary: Four legal circuits, four 'major issues' verdicts, and one shared root cause: three of the four quoted corner radii on a hug-the-inside line that has no dependence on direction change, so their corners are systematically slower on paper than in the kart. Recomputing every corner on the arc a kart actually drives reorders the field, because it deletes shallow corners entirely. Pietrarossa (instrument) wins at 80/100 on the only criterion the brief makes non-negotiable: it is the only layout whose TWO overtaking spots both survive the correction. T9 Il Tornante is 180 deg at a 14 m entry, so its line is hard-bounded at 20.3 m and nothing can open it - 220.2 m of tow through a legal straight-splitting kink, 39.4 m of braking with 51.9 m available, 126.2 m of +2.8% climb on exit - and T1 is a 12 m decreasing-radius first corner whose braking zone gets LONGER under correction, to about 35 m. Its reverse case is also the strongest and the only measured one: 2 braking zones over 20 m forward against 6 reversed, and a passing place at T7 that provably does not exist the other way. What it loses is its own thesis - four of its ten corners are flat kinks, so the eleven-rung radius ladder and the fine lap-time gradient are largely not there. Valdirone (rhythm) is second at 78 and is the better LAP: it is the only proposal that designed to direction change rather than radius, so its corner inventory is the only one that survives intact, and T3 Il Pozzo is the best single corner anybody built - 45.0 m of braking to a 52 km/h first-gear apex at 140 deg through 12 m, exiting onto 186.7 m of climb. It loses on count: T1's braking zone is 12.0 m, so it is a place a pass gets resolved rather than created, and one-and-a-half is not two. Sabliere (racecraft) is third at 68 with the best structural idea in the exercise - two 12 m corners each flanked by maximum-legal straights, with their compounds inverting sense so the reverse lap trades the dive-bomb for the drive-away - wrapped around defensive-penalty numbers that are 2x to 30x overstated and, at T1, inverted: the correctly computed pinned line (51.50 m) is WIDER than the author's own free line (48.85 m). It also has a 380 m run with no braking event in it, which is a quarter of the lap as transport, and at 186 m per corner it reads as a scaled-down road course - the exact failure the brief names. Cava Vecchia (terrain) is fourth at 47 on the best reasoning and the worst circuit: the quarry-bench argument for where elevation is allowed to live is the most valuable thing produced by anybody, and the T4 width-from-the-sweep derivation is the best-argued number, but both of its overtaking spots evaporate on the correct line (T4 is a 67.7 m line at ~126 km/h, T7 a 46.0 m line at ~101 km/h, T2 is flat at 123 m), it has zero verified braking zones over 20 m in either direction, and its reverse layout is illegal in the exact way the author spends a section claiming to have fixed. Graft onto Pietrarossa: rhythm's T4/T5 esse angles to rescue Le Esse, rhythm's 45 m hairpin approach, terrain's uphill-blind braking to give T10 La Cesta a reason to exist, terrain's width-from-the-sweep method for T1 and T9, and racecraft's compound sense-inversion so the reverse lap gets its own dive-bomb.
